approved_text: Is it true that for all natural numbers k1 ≥ k2 ≥ 3, there are only finitely many pairs of natural numbers (n1, n2) with n2 ≥ n1 + k1 such that (n1+1)(n1+2)…(n1+k1) and (n2+1)(n2+2)…(n2+k2) have exactly the same set of prime factors?
draft: Is it true that for all natural numbers k1 ≥ k2 ≥ 3, there are only finitely many pairs of natural numbers (n1, n2) with n2 ≥ n1 + k1 such that (n1+1)(n1+2)…(n1+k1) and (n2+1)(n2+2)…(n2+k2) have exactly the same set of prime factors?
source_docstrings:
Let $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2\geq n_1 + k_1$
such that
$$
  \prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(n_1 + i)\ \text{and}\ \prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2} (n_2 + j)
$$
have the same prime factors?
source_lean:
theorem erdos_931 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (k₁ : ℕ) (k₂ ≥ 3), k₂ ≤ k₁ →
    { (n₁, n₂) | n₁ + k₁ ≤ n₂ ∧
      (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (n₁ + i)).primeFactors =
      (∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (n₂ + j)).primeFactors }.Finite
